newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Fischler to seek unchanged farm prices, slash aid.
newsitem.headline: Fischler to seek unchanged farm prices, slash aid.

text.p: Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler is expected on Wednesday to propose unchanged prices in 1997/98 (July/June) but to seek cuts of 1.5 billion Ecus in mainly cereals and oilseeds aids, EU agricultural sources said.
"A farm price rollover is expected to go through," a Commission source said as the chief aides to the 20 EU commissioners were putting final touches to the package.
But Fischler is likely to meet fierce opposition from farm ministers to his insistence on 1.4 billion Ecus of cuts in farmers' compensatory payments.
An additional 130 million Ecus would be saved mainly through lower cereals monthly storage increments and a reduction in the monthly sugar storage refund.
The reductions in cereals and oilseeds compensatory payments would consist of cuts of seven percent and four percent respectively as well as a 27 percent cut in set-aside aid.
German Farm Minister Jochen Borchert warned last week that the proposed cuts would threaten the survival of many farms in Germany and other EU member states.
He said the move would break promises made in the EU's 1992 farm reform agreement that the compensatory payments would be permanent.

The proposal, first made last summer to help fund beef costs arising from the mad cow crisis, was unceremoniously dumped in October by farm ministers who found alternative savings by delaying oilseed aid payments.

Agricultural sources noted that the cuts would be much smaller than the original target of 2.6 billion Ecus. The cuts had been deemed necessary to meet strict 1998 budget limits and criteria set for the planned EU single currency.

A stronger dollar, lower cereal aid payments than projected and a 20 percent rise in sheepmeat prices over the past year have enabled the Commission to revise budget forecasts made in late 1996, they added.
But some commissioners, notably the British and Swedish, had strongly resisted Fischler's campaign to ease the pain for farmers and were insisting on stringent spending controls, the sources added.
Cuts in area payments of just over 5.5 percent for flax, and 7.5 percent for hemp are also envisaged in 1997/98.

Virtually all the three percent growth foreseen in the EU budget in 1998 has been earmarked for regional development and other structural spending. It would allow only a 0.5 percent rise in the 1998 farm budget to 41 billion Ecus.
EU aid payments to cereals and oilseed farmers total 16 to 17 billion Ecus annually, representing 40 percent of the farm budget and 20 percent of total EU expenditure.
